title: Abstract classes: no boat is just a boat

terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. Run the takings here, and try your vessels from main.

tasks.title: Write Vessel, which no boat is just by itself
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 1`, write an abstract class `Vessel` with a `private String name`, a constructor `Vessel(String name)`, a method `String getName()`, an abstract method `int fareFor(int age)` that every kind of vessel writes, and a method `String fareLine(int age)` that gives back the name and that vessel's fare for the age, as in `Linnet: 160p`.

Check writes kinds of vessel of its own that extend yours, with fares of their own, and reads what `getName` and `fareLine` give back. Then its own code tries to make a `Vessel` by itself, and to write a kind of vessel with no `fareFor`, and Java must refuse both.
nextSteps: Read the parts of the lesson about abstract classes and abstract methods.
Write the class with abstract in front, its field, its constructor and getName.
Write fareFor as an abstract method: a first line and no body.
Write fareLine so that it uses fareFor, whatever kind of vessel it is.
hints: Vessel does not know any fare: each kind of vessel does. Vessel only says that every kind has one.
An abstract method has abstract in front and ends with a semicolon where the body would be. fareLine can still call it: the kind of vessel the object really is answers.
The two lines that matter: `abstract int fareFor(int age);` and, in fareLine, `return name + ": " + fareFor(age) + "p";`.

tasks.title: Write Ferry and WaterTaxi, each with its own fare
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 2`, write a class `Ferry` and a class `WaterTaxi`, each extending `Vessel`, each with a constructor that takes the name. On a ferry under 16 pay 160 and everyone else 320. The water taxi charges 600 whatever the age.

Check runs your classes beside a `Vessel` of its own, written as Task 1 asks, so this task is judged on its own lines. It makes ferries and water taxis, keeps them in variables and a list of type `Vessel`, and reads what `fareFor`, `getName` and `fareLine` give back.
nextSteps: Read the part of the lesson about writing the abstract method in each child.
Write Ferry: its first line, a constructor that hands the name to Vessel, and fareFor.
Write WaterTaxi the same way, with its own fareFor.
Take the // off the first lines in main and run the file.
hints: Each class needs only two things: a constructor and its own fareFor.
The constructor's first line hands the name to Vessel's constructor. fareFor has exactly Vessel's first line, without abstract, with @Override above it and a body.
Ferry's fareFor gives back 160 when age is below 16 and 320 otherwise; WaterTaxi's is one line, `return 600;`.

tasks.title: Add up a day of trips on any kind of vessel
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 3`, write a class `DayTrips` with a method `static int cost(ArrayList<Vessel> trips, int age)`. It gives back what one passenger of that age pays for all the trips in the list, each at its own vessel's fare, and 0 for an empty list.

Check runs your class beside a `Vessel` of its own and with kinds of vessel of its own, whose fares you have never seen, and reads what `cost` gives back for different lists and ages.
nextSteps: Read the part of the lesson about a list of the parent's type.
Write the class and the first line of cost exactly as the task gives it.
Walk the list and add each trip's fare for the age.
Take the // off the last lines in main and run the file.
hints: cost does not need to know what kind each vessel is. Each one knows its own fare.
A for-each loop over the list gives one Vessel at a time; calling fareFor on it runs the fare of the kind it really is.
Start a total at 0, add `trip.fareFor(age)` for each trip in the list, and give back the total.
